title: Managing Exponential Complexity in Probabilistic Queryland Graphs
description: This text discusses the significant computational challenges that arise when traversing large, probabilistic graph structures, specifically focusing on the exponential explosion of nodes and edges as query length increases. The core issue is determining how to efficiently perform spanning queries in massive probabilistic graphs.
summary: The primary challenge discussed is the exponential complexity involved in querying a massive NOLI graph. If a query has length $L$ and each step involves a non-trivial expansion of nodes, the total number of nodes visited grows exponentially. This complexity is compounded by the presence of probabilistic computing edges, requiring the system to track and manage these probabilistic edges. Consequently, spanning queries in such large, probabilistic graph structures becomes a very hard computational task.

title: Handling and Answering Path Queries in Structured Data
description: This segment discusses how queries can be presented in various formats (natural language, logical formulas, graphical structures) and focuses on the system's ability to answer complex path queries. A key emphasis is placed on the capability to answer queries at test time without needing to see them during training.
summary: The discussion addresses different ways queries can be structured, including natural language, logical formulas, and graphical structures. The speaker clarifies that the focus is not on converting natural language to a formula, but on using the existing logical or graphical structure to answer a query. A crucial point is the ability to handle "path queries," asserting that the system can answer any path query regardless of the relations defined on the path. Furthermore, the method is designed such that it can answer any query at test time, meaning the query does not need to be seen during the training phase. Finally, the method must also be capable of transcribing speech segments in their original language.

title: Knowledge Graph Querying and Path Traversal
description: This segment discusses how to formulate and execute complex queries within a knowledge graph structure, focusing on predicting entities linked through specific relationships. It contrasts simple one-hop queries with multi-step path queries.
summary: The speaker introduces the concept of using knowledge graphs for prediction, specifically defining one-hop and longer path queries. One-hop queries involve starting with an entity and traversing a single relation (e.g., Fulvestrant $\rightarrow$ Causes $\rightarrow$ Associated $\rightarrow$ Protein). For more complex questions, the method involves chaining multiple relations (e.g., Breast Cancer $\rightarrow$ Treated By $\rightarrow$ Migraine $\rightarrow$ Caused By $\rightarrow$ Drug). The core idea is to define the query based on the graph structure—starting with an anchor entity and following specific relations to find the desired end entity (the answer).

title: Knowledge Graph Completion for Complex Biomedical Querying
description: This discussion focuses on using knowledge graphs, structured with biomedical entities like drugs, diseases, and proteins, to answer complex queries. The main challenge is dealing with the incompleteness of these graphs, requiring knowledge graph completion techniques to infer missing connections.
summary: The discussion introduces a biomedical knowledge graph comprising nodes for drugs, diseases, adverse events, and proteins, highlighting their relationships. The goal is to answer complex queries, such as finding all side effects caused by a specific drug. A simple traversal approach is deemed too costly and inefficient, and simple traversal fails because the knowledge graph is incomplete, meaning potential answers might be missed (e.g., missing a path through a protein). To overcome this limitation, the solution proposed is Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC), which aims to estimate and predict missing links between the head and tail of a relation type ($R$), enabling more accurate and complete answering of complex queries over incomplete biomedical knowledge.

title: Multi-Hop Reasoning in Knowledge Graphs using Embeddings
description: This lecture introduces methods for performing multi-hop and logical reasoning within Knowledge Graphs (KGs) by leveraging embeddings. The focus is on using these techniques to enable complex predictions and answers in knowledge graph structures.
summary: The session introduces the topic of reasoning over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) using embeddings, focusing on how to perform multi-hop reasoning. The core goal is to enable complex predictions and answers in KGs, allowing systems to handle multi-hop queries and arbitrary predictive queries. The specific areas covered include Path Queries, Conjunctive Queries, and Query2box. A key shift discussed is moving from a simple one-step prediction task to a multi-step prediction task, where the focus is on predicting the entity that serves as the answer to a given query within the knowledge graph.

title: Structuring End-Hop Path Queries
description: This segment explains the methodology for defining end-hop path queries, which involve traversing a sequence of relations from an anchor node to a target protein. It details how these queries are structured using specific link types (green and red) to trace causality and ultimately arrive at a given protein.
summary: The speaker defines an end-hop path query (Q) as a sequence of relations (R1 to RN) starting from a fixed entity, such as a 'visa bay' anchor node (analogous to a fullvest strand). To answer the query, the process involves traversing the path by first following the "green links" to identify the causal factors (what causes this) and then following the "red links." Finally, the path is continued along the second part of the link to arrive at the desired target protein.

title: Identifying Causal Relationships in Biological Pathways
description: This segment discusses the challenges in discovering unknown causal relationships within biological systems and the methods required to establish these connections. It uses examples from molecular pathways to illustrate how specific proteins can serve as the key answer to complex biological queries.
summary: The speaker is discussing the methodology for finding missing causal relationships, particularly when determining if one factor (e.g., fullwestrant) causes another effect (e.g., shortness of breath). They highlight the difficulty in discovering these links if pathways are not fully known or if necessary connections cannot be traversed. The discussion shifts toward the importance of identifying specific molecular components, such as caspase, as the definitive answer to a given biological query.

title: Knowledge Graph Embedding and Complex Query Planning
description: This segment discusses methods for embedding knowledge graphs to enable reasoning and navigation. It introduces the "query to box" method, framing complex path queries as predictive tasks to determine the resulting entities.
summary: The discussion focuses on how to embed knowledge graphs (KGs) so that they can be reasoned over and navigated. The approach uses a method called "query to box," where the goal is to identify the endpoint of a specific query path. This capability starts with answering simple, one-hop queries (like link prediction and KG completion). The lecture then generalizes this to answering complex path queries by chaining multiple relations. The core strategy involves formulating these complex queries as predictions, specifically predicting what entities will serve as the answer to a given query. This allows the model to handle multi-hop traversals by defining a query plan that starts at an initial entity and traverses across specific relationship types ($N$ relationships) to find the final set of resulting entities.

title: Genre Prediction via Generalized Knowledge Graph Completion
description: This work proposes extending the use of Knowledge Graphs and Knowledge Graph Completion techniques to predict an author's book genre. The approach generalizes these techniques to a more challenging setting, aiming to leverage the structural information within a knowledge graph to classify literary output.
summary: The core idea is to use knowledge graphs and knowledge graph completion methods to predict the genre of books written by a specific author. The methodology involves taking the standard concepts of knowledge graphs and knowledge graph completion and generalizing them. The goal is to extend these techniques to a more interesting and challenging domain, essentially applying the knowledge graph framework to author-to-genre prediction.
